lessons.title: Lesson 1: Being on time and ready to work
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Plan your trip and your morning so you arrive early and ready.
This lesson builds toward: For a real or practice job, you will plan your route, backup ride and morning so you arrive about 10 minutes early, with a ready-to-send message if you are late or sick.
Being on time is the first thing most supervisors notice. In many jobs, "on time" means at your station and ready to start when the shift begins, not walking in the door. Aim to arrive 10 minutes early.
Plan the trip before your first day. Check the bus or train times, or drive the route at the same time of day. Have a backup: a second bus, a ride from a friend, or money for a ride app. Set two alarms.
If you will be late or sick, tell your supervisor BEFORE the shift starts, using the way they asked you to (call, text or an app). Say when you will arrive or when you will be back. Not calling and not showing up (a "no call, no show") can cost you the job quickly.
Ready also means rested and prepared: the night before, lay out your clothes, ID, keys, lunch, and any tools or safety gear.
Step by step:
- Find out your exact start time and where to report.
- Plan the route and a backup route.
- Set two alarms and aim to arrive 10 minutes early.
- Save your supervisor's number and the call-out rules.
- Lay out clothes, ID, lunch and gear the night before.
Words to know:
- Shift: the set hours you are scheduled to work.
- Call out: telling your supervisor before your shift that you cannot come in or will be late.
- No call, no show: missing a shift without telling anyone; often a reason to be let go.
Try it now: Pick a real or practice job address. Plan your route there for a 7 am start, choose a backup way to get there, and write the exact text you would send your supervisor if your bus broke down.
You can now plan to arrive early and ready, and tell your supervisor the right way if you will be late or sick.

check.q: What is a backup plan for getting to work?
options: A second way to get there if your usual ride fails
check.why: A backup ride keeps you on time when something goes wrong.

check.q: Your bus breaks down and you will be 20 minutes late. What would you do?
options: Go home and skip the shift
Text or call your supervisor right away, the way they asked
Wait until the next day to explain
check.why: Telling your supervisor right away shows you are dependable.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Dress and communication at work
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Dress for the job and speak and write to a supervisor clearly and politely.
This lesson builds toward: In a new job, you will dress for the job and write clear, polite messages to a supervisor, including owning a mistake, with each message short and respectful.
Dress for the job you have. Ask before your first day: "Is there a uniform or dress code?" A warehouse may need steel-toe boots; an office may want business casual; a kitchen needs closed shoes and hair tied back. Clean, neat and safe is always right.
Talk with respect to everyone: supervisors, coworkers and customers. Listen to the whole instruction, repeat it back if it is long ("So you want the pallets moved to bay 3 before lunch?"), and ask when you are not sure. Asking is better than guessing and doing it wrong.
If you disagree or make a mistake, stay calm and speak privately. Own a mistake quickly: say what happened, what you did to fix it, and what you will do next time. This builds trust.
Written messages at work should be short and clear: a greeting, what you need, and your name. Avoid slang, all capitals and emojis with a supervisor until you know what is normal there.
Step by step:
- Ask about the dress code before day one.
- Listen to the whole instruction.
- Repeat long instructions back to check.
- Ask when you are not sure.
- Own mistakes quickly and privately.
- Keep work messages short: greeting, need, name.
Words to know:
- Dress code: the rules for what to wear at a job.
- Business casual: neat clothes that are less formal than a suit, such as slacks and a collared shirt.
Try it now: Write a short text to a supervisor asking a question about tomorrow's shift. Then write a two-sentence message owning a small mistake, such as putting stock in the wrong aisle, and saying how you fixed it.
You can now dress for the job and communicate with a supervisor clearly and respectfully, including owning a mistake.

check.q: What is the best way to check you understood a long instruction?
options: Repeat it back in your own words
check.why: Repeating it back catches mistakes before they happen.

check.q: You broke a box of glasses while stocking. What would you do?
options: Wait to see if anyone notices
Tell your supervisor what happened and what you did about it
check.why: Owning a mistake and saying how you fixed it builds trust.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Phone use at work
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Follow a simple phone rule that keeps you safe and focused at work.
This lesson builds toward: For your next shift, you will write a phone rule that keeps you safe and focused at work, with no phone use while driving or using machines.
Many people lose jobs over phones. Learn your workplace's phone policy on day one. Some jobs let you keep it in a pocket on silent; some ask you to leave it in a locker; some ban phones on the floor because they are a safety risk near machines, vehicles or food.
A simple rule that works almost everywhere: phone on silent and away while you work; check it only on breaks and in break areas. Never use it while driving a forklift, using a machine, or serving a customer.
If you are waiting for an important call, such as a family emergency or a call from your parole officer, a doctor or your child's school, tell your supervisor at the start of the shift and ask how they want you to handle it.
Be careful what you post. Do not post photos of the workplace, customers or coworkers, or complaints about them, without knowing the rules. It can break company policy and privacy rules.
Step by step:
- Ask about the phone policy on your first day.
- Set your phone to silent and put it away while working.
- Check it on breaks in break areas.
- Tell your supervisor ahead if you must take an important call.
- Do not post photos of the workplace or people without permission.
Words to know:
- Phone policy: the workplace's rules for when and where you can use a phone.
- Break: a set rest time during a shift.
Try it now: Write your personal phone rule for your next shift in one sentence. Then write what you would say to a supervisor if you are waiting for an important call from your child's school.
You can now follow a phone rule that keeps you safe and focused, and handle an important call the right way.

check.q: Which is a good personal phone rule for most jobs?
options: Phone on silent and away while working; check it on breaks
Phone in hand at all times
Use earbuds for music while serving customers
check.why: Silent and away during work, checked on breaks, keeps you focused.

check.q: You are driving a forklift and your phone buzzes. What would you do?
options: Ignore it until you have safely stopped and are on a break
check.why: Phone use while driving or using machines is never safe.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Your rights at work in the US

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Minimum wage, overtime and your pay stub
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check that your pay is right by comparing your hours to your pay stub.
This lesson builds toward: Given your hours log and a pay stub, you will calculate your pay, including overtime, and check it against the pay stub, raising any difference with payroll using your hours log.
The federal Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) sets a minimum wage and overtime pay for most workers. The US Department of Labor's Wage and Hour Division says the federal minimum wage is $7.25 an hour. Many states and cities set a higher minimum. When they do, the employer must pay the higher one. Check your state on dol.gov.
Overtime: unless your job is exempt, you must get at least one and a half times your regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. A workweek is a fixed seven-day period, and hours cannot be averaged across two weeks. Weekend or holiday work is not overtime by itself under federal law. Some states have extra overtime rules.
Your pay stub shows your hours, pay rate, gross pay (before deductions), deductions such as taxes, and net pay (what you take home). Federal law requires employers to keep accurate records of hours and pay, but it does not require pay stubs; many states do. Keep your own log of the days and hours you work and compare it with every stub.
If your pay is wrong, ask payroll or your supervisor politely first, with your hours log. If it is not fixed, you can contact the Wage and Hour Division or your state labor office. The FLSA makes it illegal to fire or punish you for filing a wage complaint, spoken or written.
Step by step:
- Write down the time you start and stop each day, and your breaks.
- When you get paid, find the hours, rate, gross pay, deductions and net pay on the stub.
- Check the hours match your log and the rate is what you were promised.
- Check overtime: hours over 40 in the week paid at 1.5 times your rate (unless exempt).
- If something is wrong, ask payroll with your log; if not fixed, contact the Wage and Hour Division or your state labor office.
Words to know:
- Minimum wage: the lowest hourly pay the law allows.
- Overtime: extra pay, at least 1.5 times your rate, for hours over 40 in a workweek for most hourly workers.
- Exempt: a job, often salaried and managerial, that the law does not require to get overtime.
- Gross pay: your pay before taxes and deductions.
- Net pay: what you take home after deductions.
Official sources:
- US Department of Labor: Minimum wage
- US Department of Labor: State minimum wage laws
- US Department of Labor: Overtime pay
- US Department of Labor: FLSA questions and answers (pay stubs and records)
- US Department of Labor: Fact Sheet 77A, retaliation under the FLSA
Try it now: Practice: you earn $16 an hour and worked 44 hours this week (not exempt). Work out the pay: 40 x $16, plus 4 hours x $24. Then look up your state's minimum wage on the dol.gov state page and write it down.
You can now check your hours and pay against your pay stub, spot missing overtime, and know where to go if your pay is wrong.

check.q: What is gross pay on a pay stub?
check.why: Gross pay is before deductions; net pay is what you take home.

check.q: You earn $16 an hour and worked 42 hours (not exempt). How would you work out the pay?
check.why: Overtime hours over 40 are paid at least 1.5 times the rate, so $24 here.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Discrimination and harassment, and how to report them
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Recognize workplace discrimination and harassment and know the steps to report it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a case of possible discrimination or harassment, you will list the steps to document and report it, inside the company and to the EEOC, in the right order and within the filing deadline.
Federal law, enforced by the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), makes it illegal to treat workers or applicants worse because of race, color, religion, sex (including sexual orientation, transgender status and pregnancy), national origin, age (40 or older), disability or genetic information.
Harassment is unwelcome conduct based on one of these traits. It is illegal when putting up with it becomes a condition of keeping the job, or when it is severe or frequent enough to make the workplace hostile or abusive. Examples: repeated slurs, unwanted touching, or threats.
How to report: write down what happened, when, where, who was there, and save messages. Report it using your employer's complaint process (a supervisor, manager or HR). You can also file a charge with the EEOC: online through the EEOC Public Portal, in person at an EEOC office, or start by calling 1-800-669-4000. In most cases you must file within 180 calendar days, or 300 days if a state or local agency enforces a similar law. Filing is free and you do not need a lawyer.
It is illegal for an employer to punish you (retaliate) for reporting discrimination, filing a charge, or helping in an investigation. Your state may have its own fair employment agency and extra protections.
Step by step:
- Write down what happened: date, time, place, people, words or actions.
- Save texts, emails and photos.
- Report through your employer's process: supervisor, manager or HR.
- If it is not fixed, contact the EEOC (online portal, an office, or 1-800-669-4000) or your state agency.
- Act quickly: the deadline is usually 180 days, or 300 in many states.
Words to know:
- Discrimination: treating someone worse because of a protected trait such as race, sex, age or disability.
- Harassment: unwelcome conduct based on a protected trait that is severe or frequent, or that you must accept to keep your job.
- Retaliation: punishing someone for reporting a problem or taking part in an investigation.
- EEOC: the US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, the federal agency that enforces laws against job discrimination.
Official sources:
- EEOC: How to file a charge of employment discrimination
- EEOC: Harassment
Try it now: Read this case: a coworker makes jokes about a new employee's religion every day, and the supervisor laughs. Write the first three things the new employee should do, in order, and where they could go if the company does nothing.
You can now recognize discrimination and harassment, write down what happened, and report it inside the company or to the EEOC.

options: Punishing someone for reporting a problem or using their rights
A schedule change you asked for
check.why: Retaliation is punishment for reporting or using your rights, and it is illegal.

check.q: A coworker keeps making jokes about your disability. What would you do first?
options: Write down what happened, with dates, and save any messages
check.why: Writing it down and saving messages is the first step to reporting.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: A safe workplace and where to check your state's rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain your right to a safe job, and find where to report a hazard and your state's labor office.
This lesson builds toward: Given a safety hazard or a question about state rules, you will find where to report a safety problem and your state's labor office, naming OSHA and your state labor office's website.
The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) is the federal agency for workplace safety. Employers must provide a workplace free of serious known hazards, follow safety rules, provide required safety gear, and train you about hazards in a way you understand.
You have the right to report a hazard or an injury, to ask OSHA to inspect your workplace, and to see records of work injuries. You can file a safety complaint with OSHA online, by phone at 1-800-321-OSHA (6742), by mail, or at an OSHA office, and you can ask that your name not be shared with your employer.
It is illegal to punish you for raising a safety concern or reporting an injury. If you are punished, file a retaliation (whistleblower) complaint with OSHA quickly: under federal law you have only 30 days.
State laws can add more: a higher minimum wage, paid sick leave, meal and rest breaks, pay stub rules and more. Many states run their own OSHA-approved safety plans. Find your state labor office through the Department of Labor's list of state labor offices, and check your state's own pages.
Step by step:
- Report a hazard to your supervisor first, if it is safe to do so.
- Write down what you saw and when.
- If it is not fixed, file a complaint with OSHA online or at 1-800-321-6742.
- If you are punished for reporting, file a whistleblower complaint within 30 days.
- Look up your state labor office for extra state rights.
Words to know:
- OSHA: the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety rules.
- Hazard: something at work that could hurt you, such as a wet floor, loud noise or an unguarded machine.
- Whistleblower complaint: a complaint that you were punished for reporting a problem.
Official sources:
- OSHA: File a safety and health complaint
- OSHA: Workers' rights
- OSHA Whistleblower Protection Program: file a retaliation complaint
- US Department of Labor: State labor offices
Try it now: Final task: make your one-page "Work Ready" plan. Include your arrival plan, clothes, late or sick message, phone rule, pay check routine, and where you would report unpaid wages (dol.gov), discrimination or harassment (eeoc.gov), and a safety hazard (osha.gov), plus your own state labor office's website.
You can now name your right to a safe workplace, report a hazard the right way, and find your state's extra rules.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Arrival plan No route, backup ride or alarm, or no late or sick message. Route, backup ride and alarm to arrive about 10 minutes early, plus a ready late or sick message. Times are checked on a map app and the message names who it goes to. Dress and messages Clothes not planned, or the message is unclear or rude. Clothes fit the job, and the message is short, clear and polite. Also includes how to ask about the dress code if unsure. Phone rule No phone rule, or it allows phone use while driving or on machines. A one-sentence rule that keeps the phone away while working. Also plans how to handle an important expected call. Pay check routine No hours log or pay stub check. Keeps an hours log and compares it with each pay stub, including overtime. Knows what to say to payroll if the numbers differ. Where to report Missing one of the official places, or wrong ones. Names dol.gov for wages, eeoc.gov for discrimination or harassment, and osha.gov for safety. Notes the filing deadlines and the steps to document a problem first. State labor office No state labor office listed. Lists their state labor office's website. Notes one extra right their state gives, from the official site. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which agency handles workplace safety complaints?
You want to know if your state gives paid sick leave. What would you do?
options: Ask a friend in another state
Check your state labor office, found on the Department of Labor's list
Ask an AI and trust its answer
check.why: Your state labor office has the official rules for your state.
